blocks.body:
The numbers $1, 2, \dots, 10$ are written on a board. A move erases two of them, say $a$ and $b$, and writes $|a-b|$ instead. After nine moves a single number is left. Can it be $0$? Trying move orders settles nothing. Instead notice that $a+b$ and $|a-b|$ differ by $2\min(a,b)$, so they have the same parity. Every move therefore keeps the parity of the total sum. The sum starts at $55$, which is odd, so the last number is odd. It cannot be $0$.

That one observation is the whole method. When a problem describes a process that repeats some move, look for a quantity the move does not change (an invariant) or a quantity the move always pushes the same way (a monovariant). Invariants prove that certain states can never be reached. Monovariants prove that a process must stop, and they often build the object a problem asks for.

blocks.title: Invariant and monovariant
blocks.body:
Consider a process with a set of states and a list of allowed moves, each turning a state $s$ into a new state $s'$. A function $\Phi$ on the states is an invariant if $\Phi(s') = \Phi(s)$ for every allowed move $s \to s'$. A function $\Phi$ with values in $\mathbb N = \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$ is a (decreasing) monovariant if $\Phi(s') < \Phi(s)$ for every allowed move.

In short: $\text{move} \Rightarrow \Phi(\text{state})$ unchanged, or $\Phi$ strictly decreases in $\mathbb N$. An invariant is a conserved quantity; a monovariant is a quantity that can only go downhill. (An increasing integer quantity that is bounded above works in the same way.)

blocks.title: How an invariant is used
Monovariants force termination
blocks.body: Suppose every allowed move strictly decreases a function $\Phi$ whose values are non-negative integers. Then from any starting state $s_0$, at most $\Phi(s_0)$ moves can be made in a row. In particular the process always stops.

Each move lowers $\Phi$ by at least $1$, because $\Phi$ takes integer values and strictly decreases. So after $k$ moves the value is at most $\Phi(s_0) - k$. Values are never negative, so $\Phi(s_0) - k \ge 0$, that is $k \le \Phi(s_0)$.

blocks.title: Why the values must be integers
blocks.body:
The integer condition is what makes the proof work. A quantity that strictly decreases through real numbers can do so forever: $1, \tfrac12, \tfrac14, \dots$ never reaches anything. So when you choose a monovariant, make sure it lives in $\mathbb N$, or that each move lowers it by at least some fixed amount $c > 0$ and it is bounded below.

A familiar example is sorting. Take a list of distinct numbers and repeatedly swap two neighbours that are in the wrong order. Let $\Phi$ be the number of inversions, that is pairs of positions $i < j$ whose entries are in the wrong order. Swapping a wrong-order neighbouring pair fixes exactly that pair and leaves the relative order of every other pair unchanged, so $\Phi$ drops by exactly $1$. A list of length $n$ has at most $\binom n2$ inversions, so at most $\binom n2$ swaps can ever be made, in any order. When no move is possible the list is sorted.

The Euclidean algorithm stops for the same reason: the second number of the pair $(a, b) \to (b, a \bmod b)$ is a non-negative integer that strictly decreases (see [[divisibility]]).

blocks.title: Monovariants as a construction tool
blocks.body:
Monovariants do more than prove termination. A very common pattern for existence problems runs like this. Start from any configuration. If it is not good, there is a local defect, and some move removes that defect. Show that the move strictly decreases a quantity in $\mathbb N$. Then the repairs cannot go on forever, and when they stop there is no defect left: the final configuration is the good one you wanted.

The skill is in choosing $\Phi$ so that every repair, not just a typical one, lowers it. Typical choices count bad pairs, total length, or a sum of distances.

blocks.title: A product in disguise
blocks.body: The numbers $1, 2, \dots, 20$ are written on a board. A move erases two numbers $a, b$ and writes $a + b + ab$. After $19$ moves one number remains. Which number is it, and does it depend on the order of the moves?
blocks.solution:
The key identity is $a + b + ab + 1 = (a+1)(b+1)$. So if we add $1$ to every number on the board and multiply the results, the move replaces the two factors $(a+1)(b+1)$ by the single factor $(a+b+ab)+1$, which is the same. Hence
$$\Phi = \prod_{x \text{ on the board}} (x + 1)$$
is an invariant. At the start $\Phi = 2 \cdot 3 \cdots 21 = 21!$. At the end one number $z$ remains and $\Phi = z + 1$. Therefore $z = 21! - 1$, whatever the order of moves.

blocks.title: Chameleons
blocks.body: An island has $13$ red, $15$ green and $17$ blue chameleons. When two chameleons of different colours meet, both change to the third colour; when two of the same colour meet, nothing happens. Can all $45$ chameleons eventually have the same colour?
blocks.solution:
Write the state as $(r, g, b)$. A meeting of a red and a green chameleon gives $(r-1, g-1, b+2)$. Then $r - g$ does not change, while $g - b$ and $r - b$ each change by $-3$. The other two kinds of meeting behave the same way by symmetry. So each of the three differences $r-g$, $g-b$, $r-b$ is invariant modulo $3$.

At the start $r - g = -2$, $g - b = -2$ and $r - b = -4$, which are $1, 1, 2$ modulo $3$. None of them is divisible by $3$. If all chameleons had one colour, the other two counts would both be $0$, and their difference $0$ would be divisible by $3$. That state is unreachable, so the answer is no.

We had to check all three kinds of meeting: an invariant that survives one kind of move but not another proves nothing.

blocks.title: Splitting a club
blocks.body: In a club, each member has at most three enemies among the other members (enmity is mutual). Prove that the members can be split into two groups so that everyone has at most one enemy in their own group.
blocks.solution:
Start with any split into two groups. Let $\Phi$ be the number of pairs of enemies that are in the same group; this is a non-negative integer.

Suppose some member $A$ has at least two enemies in their own group. Since $A$ has at most three enemies in total, $A$ has at most one enemy in the other group. Move $A$ to the other group. The pairs that change status are exactly those containing $A$: at least two enemy pairs stop being inside a group and at most one becomes inside a group. So $\Phi$ decreases by at least $1$.

Repeat as long as some member has two or more enemies in their own group. By the termination theorem this happens at most $\Phi(\text{start})$ times. When it stops, nobody has two enemies in their own group, which is what we wanted.

blocks.title: gcd and lcm moves
blocks.body: Several positive integers are written on a board. A move picks two numbers $a, b$ on the board such that neither divides the other, and replaces them by $\gcd(a,b)$ and $\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)$. Prove that no matter how the moves are chosen, the process stops after finitely many moves.
blocks.solution:
One preserved property and one monovariant do the job.

First, every number on the board always divides $L$, the lcm of the starting numbers: this holds at the start, and if $a \mid L$ and $b \mid L$ then $\gcd(a,b) \mid L$ and $\operatorname{lcm}(a,b) \mid L$. So every number stays at most $L$, and the sum $S$ of the numbers is at most $kL$, where $k$ is the (constant) number of entries.

Now the monovariant. Let $g = \gcd(a,b)$ and $l = \operatorname{lcm}(a,b)$. Since neither of $a, b$ divides the other, $g < a$ and $g < b$. Then $(a - g)(b - g) > 0$, which expands to $ab + g^2 > g(a+b)$. Using $ab = gl$ (true for any two positive integers) and dividing by $g$ gives $l + g > a + b$. So every move strictly increases the integer $S$, which is bounded above by $kL$. An integer that increases by at least $1$ at each step and never exceeds $kL$ can increase at most $kL$ times, so the process stops.

blocks.body:
- An invariant only proves impossibility. Equal values of $\Phi$ at the start and the target do not show that the target is reachable.
- Check every kind of move. It is easy to verify the invariant for the move you had in mind and miss another one.
- A strictly decreasing real-valued quantity does not prove termination; it needs integer values (or a fixed minimum decrease) and a lower bound.
- A quantity that merely never increases does not prove termination either: the process could cycle with $\Phi$ constant.

Invariants are the olympiad version of conserved quantities in physics, and monovariants are the loop variants that computer scientists use to prove that programs halt.

In [[comb-games]], a winning strategy keeps the game inside a set of positions (the losing positions for the opponent); that set is an invariant the winner maintains, and the analysis of Nim is exactly of this kind. In [[grids-tilings]], colouring a board and counting each colour is the main tool for showing that a tiling cannot exist. Invariants modulo $m$ are arguments in [[congruences]], and termination arguments underlie the Euclidean algorithm in [[divisibility]]. When the state space is finite, [[pigeonhole]] arguments often combine with invariants: a process that can be run backwards in a unique way must eventually return to its starting state.

1. Show that a $10 \times 10$ board cannot be tiled by $1 \times 4$ rectangles. (Find a colouring with four colours that every tile meets once each.)
2. The numbers $1, 2, \dots, 100$ are on a board. A move replaces two numbers $a, b$ by $\dfrac{ab}{a+b}$. Find the number that remains after $99$ moves.
3. Starting from the triple $(3, 4, 5)$, a move replaces two of the numbers $x, y$ by $\dfrac{x+y}{\sqrt2}$ and $\dfrac{x-y}{\sqrt2}$. Can you reach a triple containing $6$ and $7$?
4. A row of coins shows heads and tails. A move picks a head that is not the last coin in the row, turns it to tails and flips the coin immediately to its right. Prove that the process always stops.
